Instructional Team

Course Description

Calendar Description for MATH 115

Linear equations, matrices, and determinants. Introduction to vector spaces. Eigenvalues and diagonalization. Applications. Complex numbers.

View requirements for MATH 115

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this course students should be able to...
Present solutions to problems in a clear and logical manner with all steps being fully justified. [1a]
Understand the basic operations of addition and scalar multiplication as they apply to vectors, matrices and linear transformations. [1a]
Solve geometric problems using vectors, lines, and planes. [1a]
Find the solution to a system of linear equations using matrices and elementary row operations. [1a]
Understand matrix algebra and its connection to systems of equations. [1a]
Have both a geometric and an algebraic understanding of span, linear independence, bases and subspaces. [1a]
Recognize the link between matrices and linear transformations, and understand that many common geometric operations such as projections, reflections and rotations are linear transformations. [1a]
Evaluate determinants, and use them to determine if a matrix is invertible and to compute areas and volumes. [1a]
Develop a basic algebraic and geometric understanding of complex numbers and complex polynomials. [1a]
Determine the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix and diagonalize a matrix. [1a]

Tentative Class Plan

Course introduction and overview

Chapter 1 Vector Geometry

     1.1 Vectors in Rn

     1.2 Linear Combinations

     1.3 The Norm and the Dot Product

     1.4 Vector Equations of Lines and Planes

     1.5 The Cross Product in R3

     1.6 The Scalar Equation of Planes in R3

     1.7 Projections

Chapter 2 Systems of Linear Equations

     2.1 Introduction and Terminology

     2.2 Solving Systems of Linear Equations

     2.3 Rank

     2.4 Homogeneous Systems of Linear Equations

Chapter 3 Matrices

     3.1 Matrix Algebra

     3.2 The Matrix-Vector Product

     3.3 The Matrix Equation Ax=b

     3.4 Matrix Multiplication

     3.5 Matrix Inverses

Chapter 4 Subspaces of Rn

     4.1 Spanning Sets

     4.2 Geometry of Spanning Sets

     4.3 Linear Dependence and Linear Independence

     4.4 Subspaces of Rn

     4.5 Bases and Dimension

     4.6 Fundamental Subspaces of a Matrix

Chapter 5 Linear Transformations

     5.1 Matrix Transformations and Linear Transformations

     5.2 Examples of Linear Transformations

     5.3 Operations on Linear Transformations

     5.4 Inverses of Linear Transformations

     5.5 The Kernel and the Range

Chapter 6 Determinants

     6.1 Determinants and Invertibility

     6.2 Elementary Row and Column Operations

     6.3 Properties of Determinants

Chapter 7 Complex Numbers

     7.1 Basic Operations

     7.2 Conjugate and Modulus

     7.3 Polar Form

     7.4 Complex Polynomials

     7.5 Complex nth Roots

Chapter 8 Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors

     8.1 Introduction

     8.2 Computing Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors

     8.3 Eigenspaces

     8.4 Diagonalization

     8.5 Powers of Matrices

Additional topics at the discretion of the instructor (as time permits)

Grading Scheme 2
Component / Activity Date or Due Date Location / Submission Method Weight (%)
Weekly Tutorial Assignments 10%

Midterm 25%
Final Exam 60%

Grade Calculation: A student must achieve a weighted average of at least 50% on the combined midterm and final exam to pass the course. Specifically, letting M be the student's midterm percentage and F be the student's final exam percentage, we compute the exam averages under both schemes:

x1​=(30M+55F)/85 (Grading Scheme 1 exam average)
x2​=(25M+60F)/85 (Grading Scheme 2 exam average)

If x=max{x1​,x2​} is less than 50, then x will be the student's final grade in the course. If x is 50 or greater, then the student's course grade will be the higher of Grading Scheme 1 and Grading Scheme 2.

Weekly Tutorial Assignments: There will be approximately 9 equally weighted weekly tutorial assignments. Each tutorial will feature a graded problem set designed to make students think critically about the course content.  The tutorial assignment will contain computational problems, questions that require making connections to previous weeks' material, and questions that require you to prove or disprove mathematical statements.  It is strongly recommended that you prepare for the tutorials in advance by attempting the practice problems presented at the end of each section of the course notes.  Students looking for extra practice beyond the course notes are welcome to attempt problems in the corresponding sections of the optional textbook.

  • Due Date: Tutorial assignments need to be completed within the timeslot of the tutorial, in the assigned tutorial room.  You may not attend a tutorial section that you are not enrolled in, and you may not complete the tutorial assignment at an alternate time.  The tutorial assignment questions will be given to you at the beginning of your tutorial, and your completed solutions must be submitted (on paper; electronic submissions will not be accepted) by the end of the tutorial session. Tutorials will begin on September 16 - there are no tutorials before then.

  • Group Work on Tutorial Assignments: You may solve the problems in a group of up to 3 people, or individually if you prefer. If working in a group, you must indicate on your assignment who you worked with. Each group member must write and submit their own solutions, in their own words. The goal in allowing you to work with other students is to help with the learning process; so long as you are discussing the concepts and teaching each other math, it is permitted.  It is NOT permitted to copy solutions that you didn’t write or do not understand, in whole or in part, including solutions written by your colleagues or others on the internet. The moral: exchanging ideas is encouraged, but the final submission must be your own work.

  • Permitted Resources: In the tutorial you are permitted to use a scientific (non-graphing) calculator. No other resources are permitted.

  • Lowest Tutorial Grade Dropped: When computing your tutorial grade, we will drop your lowest tutorial score and will only use the remaining (equally weighted) tutorial scores.  Note that tutorials omitted due to illness or other verified absences will NOT count as the dropped tutorial.

  • Tutorial Bonus: Students who attend all tutorials for their section and effortfully attempt all tutorial assignments will receive a 1% bonus to their final course grade provided they achieve a weighted average of at least 50% on the combined midterm and final exam (see the note on Grade Calculations above). Verified absences that are properly reported and approved by your instructor will not prevent you from earning the tutorial bonus.

  • Unclaimed Tutorial Assignments: Any tutorial assignments that are not picked up by students will be destroyed at the end of January, 2027.

Python Assignments: Throughout the term, there will be 5 equally weighted assignments where students will use python to execute some prewritten code in an effort to explore some larger-scale applications of linear algebra.  No prior experience programming in python is necessary.  

  • Due Date: To be determined throughout the term.  Students will be given a full week to work on assignments.

  • Best 4 of 5: Only your best 4 out of the 5 python assignments will count towards your final grade.  Note that assignments omitted due to illness or other verified absences will NOT count as the dropped assignment.

Midterm Exam: A 90 minute (1.5 hour) midterm exam will be held on Monday, October 26 from 8:00pm to 9:30pm.  More information regarding this exam will appear later in the semester.

Final Exam: A 150 minute (2.5 hour) cumulative final examination will be scheduled by the Registrar's Office during the examination period from Thursday, December 10, 2025 to Wednesday, December 23, 2025. Students are expected to be present during the final exam period.

Regrade Requests: Regrade requests will be handled in one of two ways:

  • Tutorial Assignments: If you believe one of your tutorial assignments was graded incorrectly, please bring this to the attention of your tutorial TA. You must be specific when asking for reconsideration of your work: requests for more marks without justification or reference to a specific question on the assignment will not be considered. A regrade may result in an increase, decrease, or no change in grade. After receiving a graded tutorial assignment, you have until the end of the next tutorial session to request a regrade. (e.g., if a graded assignment is returned to you during Tutorial 2, you have until the end of Tutorial 3 to request a regrade of this assignment.)

  • Midterm or Final Exam: If you have concerns about the grading of your midterm or final exam, please bring them to the attention of your instructor. Students have until December 8 at 4:30pm to request a regrade of their midterm.

Missed Assessments: Students have three options if they miss an assessment:

  • Declare a short-term absence (two-day absence) on absence.uwaterloo.ca.  This is available to students once during the formal lecture period and cannot be used during the final exam period.  The short-term absence can be declared for any reason and requires no documentation.  Students must declare their absence within the two-day window for which they they are requesting the accommodation.  Retroactive declaration requests will not be approved.  If a student does not submit a short-term absence at the time when it is required, then the course instructor will need to determine if accommodation is warranted given their situation.

  • Declare a religious or creed-related absence on absence.uwaterloo.ca. These can be submitted more than once during an academic term and can be used during the final exam period. No accompanying documentation is requested or required. Note however, that religious or creed-related absenses must be submitted within two weeks of the announcement of the due date or scheduled examination date for which the academic accommodation is being sought. In particular, to be exempted from the final exam, you must submit no later than two weeks after the final examination schedule is released.

  • Submit a Verification of Condition Form (VOC) to absence.uwaterloo.ca for approval by the Engineering Undergraduate Office.  These may be submitted at any time and you may do so more than once during the term.  The dates on the form must cover the date of any assessment for which the student seeks accommodation. The UWaterloo Verification of Condition form, completed by a health professional, is the only acceptable documentation for an absence due to illness. Do not send any documentation to your advisor, course instructor, teaching assistant, or lab coordinator.

Notes:

  • If no documentation is submitted for a missed assessment, then the student will receive a grade of zero on that assessment.

  • Upon declaring any absence (short term, religious/creed or VIF) in an effort to be exempted from any MATH 115 assessment, you must immediately email your instructor to notify them of which assessment you will be missing or else you will not be exempted from the assessment and will receive a grade of zero instead.  

  • If you find yourself in a situation where you are missing multiple assessments, then you are advised to contact both your instructor and the First Year Engineering Office to make sure you have the proper supports in place to succeed in this courses.

Rescheduling Co-op Interviews: 

As best as possible, coop interviews should be scheduled around your academic commitments. Unavoidable tutorial conflicts with coop interviews should be communicated to your instructor by email. Attendance at coop interviews is not considered to be a valid reason to miss an exam, hence you will be expected to reschedule any co-op interviews that conflict with midterms or finals.

Late / Missed Content

Assuming adequate documentation is provided:

  • If a tutorial assignment (or a python assignment) is missed, then its weight will normally be evenly distributed among the remaining tutorial assignments (or python assignments). If a student misses several tutorials, then the instructor may, at their discretion, move the weight of the missed tutorials to the final exam instead.

  • If the midterm is missed, the weight of the midterm will be moved to the final exam.

  • If the final exam is missed, then the student may qualify for a grade of INC. A grade of INC (incomplete) will remain on the student's record until they write a MATH 115 final exam given during a future offering of the course.

Assignment Screening

The Instructor and the TAs will be comparing students' solutions with other students' solutions to screen for potential plagiarism and violations of academic integrity. Websites that offer to complete students' homework for them will also be monitored. To be clear - such websites are not allowed to be used for the completion of any part of the course MATH 115, and students are not permitted to share questions from the course anywhere.

Generative AI

Generative AI: This course includes the independent development and practice of specific skills, such as computations, problem solving and proof writing. Therefore, the use of Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) trained using large language models (LLM) or other methods to produce text, images, music, or code, like Chat GPT, DALL-E, or GitHub CoPilot, is not permitted in this class. Unauthorized use in this course, such as running course materials through GenAI or using GenAI to complete a course assessment is considered a violation of Policy 71 (plagiarism or unauthorized aids or assistance). Work produced with the assistance of AI tools does not represent the author’s original work and is therefore in violation of the fundamental values of academic integrity including honesty, trust, respect, fairness, responsibility and courage (ICAI, n.d.). 

You should be prepared to show your work. To demonstrate your learning, you should keep your rough notes, including research notes, brainstorming, and drafting notes. You may be asked to submit these notes along with earlier drafts of their work, either through saved drafts or saved versions of a document. If the use of GenAI is suspected where not permitted, you may be asked to meet with your instructor or TA to provide explanations to support the submitted material as being your original work. Through this process, if you have not sufficiently supported your work, academic misconduct allegations may be brought to the Associate Dean. 

In addition, you should be aware that the legal/copyright status of generative AI inputs and outputs is unclear. More information is available from the Copyright Advisory Committee:  https://uwaterloo.ca/copyright...

Diversity: It is our intent that students from all backgrounds and perspectives be well served, and that students’ learning needs be addressed both in and out of class. We recognize the immense value of the diversity in identities, perspectives, and contributions that students bring, and the benefit it has on our educational environment. In particular:

  • We will follow AccessAbility Services guidelines and protocols on how to best support students with different learning needs.
     

Territorial Acknowledgement: The University of Waterloo acknowledges that much of our work takes place on the traditional territory of the Neutral, Anishinaabeg and Haudenosaunee peoples. Religious & Spiritual Observances: The University of Waterloo has a duty to accommodate religious and spiritual observances under the Ontario Human Rights Code. Consult with your instructor(s) within two weeks of the announcement of the due date for which accommodation is being sought. 


Continuity Plan - Fair Contingencies for Unforeseen Circumstances (e.g., resurgence of COVID-19): In the event of emergencies or highly unusual circumstances, the instructor will collaborate with the Department/Faculty to find reasonable and fair solutions that respect rights and workloads of students, staff, and faculty. This may include modifying content delivery, course topics and/or assessments and/or weight and/or deadlines with due and fair notice to students. Substantial changes after the first week of classes require the approval of the Associate Dean, Undergraduate Studies.

Accreditation Data Collection

The Faculty of Engineering may be collecting information from this course for accreditation purposes, including course outline, exams, assignments, and samples of student work. The Canadian Engineering Accreditation Board (CEAB) periodically reviews the Bachelor of Applied Science (BASc) and the Bachelor of Software Engineering (BSE) degrees. The Canadian Architectural Certification Board (CACB) periodically reviews the Bachelor of Architectural Studies (BAS) degree and the Master of Architecture (MArch) degree.

University Policy

Mental Health: At the University of Waterloo, we are dedicated to supporting your mental and emotional well-being. Our Counselling Services offer confidential support, including individual counselling, workshops, and crisis intervention.
If you're struggling, please reach out for help at 519-888-4096 or visit their website for more information.

Academic integrity: In order to maintain a culture of academic integrity, members of the University of Waterloo community are expected to promote honesty, trust, fairness, respect and responsibility.

Grievance: A student who believes that a decision affecting some aspect of their university life has been unfair or unreasonable may have grounds for initiating a grievance. Read Policy 70, Student Petitions and Grievances, Section 4. When in doubt, please be certain to contact the department’s administrative assistant who will provide further assistance.

Discipline: A student is expected to know what constitutes academic integrity to avoid committing an academic offence, and to take responsibility for their actions. A student who is unsure whether an action constitutes an offence, or who needs help in learning how to avoid offences (e.g., plagiarism, cheating) or about “rules” for group work/collaboration should seek guidance from the course instructor, academic advisor, or the undergraduate associate dean. For information on categories of offences and types of penalties, students should refer to Policy 71, Student Discipline. For typical penalties, check Guidelines for the Assessment of Penalties.

Appeals: A decision made or penalty imposed under Policy 70, Student Petitions and Grievances (other than a petition) or Policy 71, Student Discipline may be appealed if there is a ground. A student who believes they have a ground for an appeal should refer to Policy 72, Student Appeals.

Note for students with disabilities and disabling conditions: The University of Waterloo recognizes its obligations under the Ontario Human Rights Code to accommodate students with known or suspected disabilities and disabling conditions (e.g. medical conditions, injuries, impacts of trauma such as from violence or discrimination) to the point of undue hardship. To support this obligation, AccessAbility Services (AAS) collaborates with all academic departments and schools to facilitate academic accommodations for students with disabilities and disabling conditions without compromising the academic integrity of the curriculum. If you believe you may require academic accommodations (e.g., testing accommodations, classroom accommodations), register with AAS as early in the term as possible by completing the online application. Students already registered with AAS must activate their accommodations for each of their courses at the beginning of each term using AAS' online system. If you require assistance, contact AAS by phone (519-888-4567 ext. 35082), email (instructor@example.com) or in-person (Needles Hall North, 1st Floor, Room 1401). 

Turnitin.com: Text matching software (Turnitin®) may be used to screen assignments in this course. Turnitin® is used to verify that all materials and sources in assignments are documented. Students' submissions are stored on a U.S. server, therefore students must be given an alternative (e.g., scaffolded assignment or annotated bibliography), if they are concerned about their privacy and/or security. Students will be given due notice, in the first week of the term and/or at the time assignment details are provided, about arrangements and alternatives for the use of Turnitin in this course.

It is the responsibility of the student to notify the instructor if they, in the first week of term or at the time assignment details are provided, wish to submit alternate assignment.
